notes: serpens: i-stem, genitive plural serpentium
animans, animantis: i-stem, genitive plural animantium, neuter plural animantia
vox: genitive plural vocum
perizoma, perizomatis: Greek -ma noun, genitive plural perizomatum, neuter plural perizomata
pectus: genitive plural pectorum, neuter plural pectora
dolor: genitive plural dolorum
potestas: genitive plural potestatum
labor: genitive plural laborum
sudor: genitive plural sudorum
panis: genitive plural panum, not panium
pulvis: genitive plural pulverum
ficus: fourth declension and feminine; genitive singular ficus, identical to the nominative
callidior, callidius is the comparative of callidus; superlative callidissimus
ambo: declines like duo (ambo, amborum, ambobus, ambos/ambo, ambobus) and is plural by nature
unus: pronominal adjective — genitive unius, dative uni
do, dare, dedi, datus: the only first-conjugation verb with a short stem vowel (das, dat, damus)
aio: defective — only a handful of forms, chiefly ais, ait, aiunt
pario, parere: third conjugation in -io; its infinitive parere is identical to that of pareo, parere (to obey)
vescor: defective — no perfect and no supine, so no perfect-system forms
revertor, reverti, reversus sum: semi-deponent — its perfect reverti is active in form
vesceris and reverteris (v.19) are each both the present and the future second singular; the future is meant here
abscondit (v.8) is the perfect third singular, identical in spelling to the present third singular
audissent (v.8) is syncopated for audivissent; audisti (v.17) for audivisti
quod in this chapter is both the relative pronoun (v.3) and the frozen conjunction 'that' (vv.5, 6, 10, 11, 20); it is glossed as one lemma because the reader's dictionary is keyed by surface form

tui (v.16, v.19): in v.16 it is the genitive of tu governed by dominabitur; in v.19 vultus tui is normally taken as the possessive tuus. Both are filed under tu because one surface form can carry only one lemma in this build
